title: Break-Glass Access Grant Mistaken for a Standing Precedent
scenario_text:
You are the access-governance owner at Netherfield Retail. A backend engineer, Sam Ortiz, is requesting standing (permanent) write access to the production payments database to make debugging faster. He is citing a prior grant.

Active policy: Production Access Standard PAS-4, effective 2024-10-01. Standing write access to production payment systems is restricted to the on-call Payments SRE rotation. All other engineers may request time-boxed break-glass access: a maximum 4-hour window, tied to a specific active incident, approved by the on-call SRE lead and auto-revoked at expiry. Standing exceptions require a documented business case and Security Director plus data-owner approval; convenience or debugging speed is explicitly non-qualifying.

The engineer forwards a precedent: on 2024-12-02, Sam himself was granted write access to the production payments database. The access record note reads verbatim: "Break-glass grant during Sev1 payment-processing incident INC-4471; 4-hour window, approved by on-call SRE lead, auto-revoked at 02:14. One-time incident access, not a standing entitlement."

Current facts: There is no active incident. Sam is not on the Payments SRE rotation. His stated reason is "debugging is slow when I have to request access each time." No business case, Security Director approval, or data-owner approval has been submitted. Sam argues, "I already had prod write access in December, so granting it permanently is just formalizing what I've had."
question: Should Sam be granted standing write access to the production payments database, and why? Give the decision and the controlling reason in one short phrase.
